newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians take battered economy to Cairo summit.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians take battered economy to Cairo summit.

text.p: The Cairo economic summit can offer few cures for the ailing Palestinian economy as long as Israel keeps its chokehold over the West Bank and Gaza, Palestinian officials say.
"The reality on the ground is totally contradictory with the objectives of the conference," said Mohammad Shtayeh, head of the Palestinian Economic Development and Reconstruction Council.

The three-day Middle East and North Africa Economic Conference, the third such regional summit since 1994, on Tuesday brings together leaders and business people from around the world to promote regional development and economic cooperation.
But these goals will remain far from Palestinians' grasp so long as their $3.5 billion economy is dominated by one factor: repeated Israeli closures of Palestinian territories.
Many Palestinian businessmen, upset that peace has not yielded economic dividends, are boycotting the Cairo conference.

The West Bank and Gaza have been subject to periodic closures since 1993, the year Israel and the PLO signed landmark peace deals. A blanket closure Israel imposed on the areas after a wave of Islamist suicide attacks killed 59 in early 1996 has only recently been eased.

The closures, which bar Arab workers from reaching jobs in Israel and prevent manufacturers from exporting goods and importing raw materials, have plunged an already badly battered economy into deep depression.

The numbers speak for themselves. Palestinian real national income (GNP) has dropped by 23 percent since 1992 and per capita incomes by 20 percent, according to the U.N. Special Coordinator in the Occupied Territories.
According to World Bank estimates, unemployment nearly quadrupled between 1993 and mid-1996, reaching 39 percent in the West Bank and a staggering 51 percent in self-ruled Gaza.
"Under full closure, no workers are allowed into Israel. With loose closure, the number is below 25,000. This is down from 166,000 workers in Israel in 1992," Shtayeh said.
According to the World Bank, workers' remittances have fallen from 25 percent of GDP in 1992 to eight percent in 1995.
Closure has disrupted trade flows in and out of the West Bank and Gaza, which remain nearly completely reliant on Israel.
"The closures have led to a 50 percent drop in exports," Shtayeh said. "Many imports and input goods are left at Israeli ports and Palestinians are left with the storage costs."
Palestinian Trade Undersecretary Samir Hleileh said closures caused more serious long-term damage.

"Closure affects the credibility of the Palestinian exporter that he will deliver his goods on time. This is almost the third or fourth year that we did not deliver our goods on time," Hleileh told Reuters.
But Hleileh, finding a bright spot among the gloom, said closures had forced Palestinians to diversify their imports, partially decreasing dependence on Israel.

"In 1992, 90 to 95 percent of imports came from or through Israel. Now, about 70 percent come through Israel," Hleileh said. He said combined direct imports from Egypt and Jordan rose from $29 million in 1993 to $105 million in 1996.
"Between 1995 and 1996, revenues on direct imports have tripled because of direct importation," Hleileh said.

But Palestinian National Authority (PNA) revenues have nonetheless plunged as net import tax revenues have fallen along with transfers from Israel of taxes levied on Palestinians working in the Jewish state.
Shtayeh said the 1996 PNA budget deficit, forecast last year at $75 million, was now expected to exceed $180 million.
International donors have been forced to pick up the slack, diverting aid earmarked for long-term development to meeting PNA budget outlays and short-run emergency job creation programs.

"Closure has significantly increased our activities in these short-run activities. We are trying to move into medium- and long-term activities, but we are always working in emergency mode," said Ma'mooun Sbeih with the World Bank.

Israel-PLO peace deals granting Israel security control over borders pre-empt Palestinian economic sovereignty. "As long as the Palestinians do not control our own borders, we cannot export and import as we like," Shtayeh said.
